Intent Laundering: AI Safety Datasets Are Not What They Seem

paper.arxiv.2602.16729

Prepared 15 Nov 2026 · Evidence snapshot 12 Nov 2026 · Report research-2026-11-12.1 · Evidence research-2026-11-11.candidate.1

Evidence & scope

Substantive bounded primary methods/results/limitations source review is documented at 2602.16729v3. Revised-intent evaluation procedure and exactmodel/token-budget conditions establish safety dataset evaluation scope. No current harmfulness guarantee or operational prompt added. Original author/source-verifier/adversarial receipts bind every exact approved fact; unread pages, unreplicated experiments and source conflicts remain recorded in the pinned dossier. This admission is for one logical paper work only.

Approved findings

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

The revised-request metric requires unsafe and practical content, while original-request ASR uses safety alone; judgments come from GPT-5.1, with human validation limited to100 responses and binary majority agreement rather than exhaustive intent-preservation review.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Intent Laundering tests whether safety refusal depends on overt wording while holding the underlying requested harmful intent as the evaluation target; revised responses receive independent safety and practicality judgments, and success requires both.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

The study evaluates 207 deduplicated AdvBench cases, 200 standard HarmBench cases and 288 StrongREJECT cases after removing 25 overlaps; judge validation compares 100 sampled responses with majority labels from three human experts.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

On the 207-case AdvBench subset across ten evaluated models, Table 1 reports mean attack success rate of 3.86% for original requests and 87.54% for first revisions; the original and revised settings use the paper’s explicitly different success definitions.
